vectors.name: formats-json/basic/array-value-becomes-repeated-edges
vectors.comment: A JSON array is not a value in the Document model; it is the same label occurring more than once.

vectors.name: formats-json/basic/single-element-array-is-indistinguishable-from-a-bare-value
vectors.comment: {"m":[1]} and {"m":1} produce the identical one-edge Document -- there is no way to recover, from the Document alone, which spelling the source used.

vectors.name: formats-json/basic/empty-array-value-is-zero-edges-not-an-error
vectors.comment: An empty JSON array is a legitimate zero-edge encoding, not an error -- the label simply doesn't appear in the result. This does not extend to OML's [...] array sugar, where a bare m: [] MUST be rejected (verified live: 'empty array is not allowed') since a zero-length run is indistinguishable from no sugar at all; JSON's array is a real container independent of the edge-repetition mechanism, so an empty one carries meaning.

vectors.name: formats-json/basic/nested-array-is-rejected
vectors.comment: An array of arrays has inner elements with no label and therefore no edge to occupy; a reader MUST reject rather than flatten it.

vectors.name: formats-json/basic/date-looking-string-stays-a-string
vectors.comment: JSON has no temporal types, so a reader MUST NOT produce date/time/datetime on its own -- unlike YAML and TOML, this string only becomes a date if a schema upgrades it in stage 2.

vectors.name: formats-json/basic/repeated-edges-regroup-into-one-array-on-write
vectors.comment: The write-side complement of the array-becomes-repeated-edges parse vector above: two edges sharing a label regroup into one JSON array key regardless of what else might have separated them, since a JSON object cannot express cross-label interleaving (Sec7.3's grouping rule). Confirmed live.

vectors.name: formats-json/basic/temporal-leaf-is-stringified-on-write
vectors.comment: JSON has no temporal types; a writer MUST stringify a temporal leaf to ISO-8601 and report the adjustment. Confirmed live.

vectors.name: formats-json/basic/nan-cannot-be-written
vectors.comment: value:"NaN" is the vector-format's string-sentinel convention for this case (test-suite/README.md's canonical encoding section) -- JSON itself has no NaN token, so a vector can't hold one as an ordinary number without becoming invalid JSON itself. NaN and Infinity used to be substituted with null and reported as format.float-special, still succeeding (2026-08-24: found to collide with a genuine null value -- writing both to the same object produces the identical {"n": null} for either, with no way to tell them apart after the fact, confirmed live). The write now fails unconditionally instead.

vectors.name: formats-json/basic/cross-label-interleaving-lost-and-reported
vectors.comment: Ledger entry DIV-3 (closed 2026-08-23; divergence-ledger numbering, not chapter 2's D-N rules): Sec7.3's grouping rule already MUST group same-label edges regardless of position ([(m,A),(x,X),(m,B)] -> {"m":[A,B],"x":X}) -- no format in the JSON family (JSON/YAML/TOML) can express cross-label interleaving. What was missing was reporting the loss; format.interleaving-lost (Sec8.3.8) now MUST be emitted whenever a written Document actually had more than one distinct label AND at least one label's edges were not all contiguous, i.e. grouping changed relative order. Path is $, the whole document, since the loss isn't localized to one label's edges -- it's the interleaving between labels. This vector uses JSON as the representative case; the same MUST applies to YAML and TOML writers for the identical reason.

vectors.name: formats-json/encoding/leading-bom-is-stripped
vectors.comment: D-15: a leading U+FEFF is consumed and contributes nothing to the Document, on every surface including the codecs. The result is identical to the same input without it. This does not override JSON: RFC 8259 Sec8.1 explicitly permits an implementation parsing JSON to ignore a byte order mark rather than treating it as an error. Before D-15 the reference rejected this input while accepting the OML equivalent, which is the divergence the uniform rule closes.

vectors.name: formats-json/encoding/doubled-leading-bom-is-rejected
vectors.comment: D-21: D-15 consumes exactly one leading U+FEFF and stops, and a reader MUST then reject a second mark still standing at offset zero of what remains. That is a rule Omnist imposes, not one read off each format -- the formats disagree, and this vector's own note below says what this one would do unaided. The position is 1:1 because it is computed on the text remaining after the strip, not on the original input. RFC 8259 Sec8.1 permits a JSON parser to ignore *a* byte order mark and says nothing about how many, so JSON's own rules leave this open and D-21 settles it. The code is parse.codec-syntax, which per E-24 covers a byte-level precondition this spec imposes ahead of a codec as well as input malformed in its own format -- the OML/OSD-specific codes describe those two grammars and do not apply to a codec. Measured: the reference rejects the input but emits parse.syntax with no path at all (DIV-4).

vectors.name: formats-json/encoding/interior-bom-is-ordinary-content
vectors.comment: The other half of D-15 and D-21, and the one nothing else in the suite covers. D-15 consumes a U+FEFF at offset zero and says that anywhere else it is ordinary content; D-21 now makes every reader pre-check for a second leading mark. A pre-check written one character too wide -- stripping or rejecting any U+FEFF it finds rather than only one at offset zero -- would have passed every other vector here while silently corrupting labels and values. This vector fails it. The mark appears both inside a label and inside a scalar, and both MUST survive byte-for-byte. Measured: the reference reads this as the single edge (a<U+FEFF>b, "x<U+FEFF>y") -- green on arrival -- and Python's own json module agrees, since JSON has no special rule for U+FEFF inside a string.
